name: Obstetrics and Gynecology
boundaries: Obstetrics and Gynecology: fundamental discoveries and enabling technologies within this field. Include cross-field consequences where the central advance belongs to this field; exclude routine incremental optimization. Use the historical breakthroughs in the prompt to calibrate revolutionary impact.

original_dispositions.original_title: Prevention or cure of preeclampsia and all hypertensive disorders
original_dispositions.reason: Covered by OBG-04 for the revolutionary core: reversing established placental disease so delivery is no longer the cure. Not given a new ID. Extending the claim to every hypertensive disorder, including chronic hypertension, would attach ordinary blood-pressure treatment to a placental discovery. Aspirin prevention is already real and is distinguished inside OBG-04.

original_dispositions.original_title: Mechanism-based prevention of spontaneous preterm birth
original_dispositions.reason: Covered by OBG-01. The historical “greater than 90 percent across all etiologies” is not used. Indicated preterm birth and membrane rupture remain OBG-04 and OBG-10.
Covered by OBG-07. The requirement of no side effects is treated as a safety hope, not a separate concept.

original_dispositions.original_title: One maternal blood test at 5–6 weeks for every genetic and chromosomal disorder at greater than 99 percent accuracy
original_dispositions.reason: Not added. The principle of reading placental DNA from maternal blood is already in clinical use. SMFM Consult Series #74 recommends that cell-free DNA screening for trisomies 21, 18, and 13 “be made routinely available to all obstetrical patients,” generally from 9–10 weeks, and does not recommend routine microdeletion screening (Pregnancy, 2025; DOI 10.1002/pmf2.70139; https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/pmf2.70139, recommendations; author list not in the extract). UpToDate’s visible introduction says placental cell-free DNA can be detected as early as five weeks and that the test “is not considered diagnostic” (page updated 15 September 2025; https://www.uptodate.com/contents/prenatal-screening-for-common-fetal-aneuploidies-cell-free-dna-test, introduction; later text not accessible). Johansen Taber and Muzzey report that fetal-fraction amplification makes aneuploidy screening feasible from about 7 3/7 to 8 weeks, with limited performance data (Obstetrics & Gynecology 2026;148:149–156; DOI 10.1097/AOG.0000000000006324; https://journals.lww.com/greenjournal/fulltext/10.1097/aog.0000000000006324, conclusion). A 2026 Science Advances review states that NIPT “is currently limited to be only a screening test due to fundamental biological bottlenecks,” including low fetal fraction, distinguishing fetal from maternal DNA, and discordance with the fetal genotype (DOI 10.1126/sciadv.aef5425; https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aef5425, introduction; author list not re-retrieved). The October 2026 ASHG report of 97.2 percent detection against invasive diagnoses was a meeting release, not routine care, and not a 5–6-week test for every condition (https://www.ashg.org/publications-news/press-releases/noninvasive-fetal-exome-blood-test-detects-97-of-diagnoses-found-by-invasive-sequencing/). What remains is earlier timing, validation, and completeness of an existing method. Because the circulating DNA is placental, confined placental mosaicism is a biological limit on any claim of zero error for every fetal condition.

original_dispositions.original_title: Restoration of ovarian function and reversal of menopause
Scarless healing after cesarean or other uterine surgery
original_dispositions.reason: Not added. Placenta accreta spectrum is a serious consequence of uterine scarring. Jauniaux and colleagues write that “more than 90% of cases are now found in patients with a history of caesarean delivery” and an anterior low placenta or previa, and that accreta reflects loss of normal signaling and mechanics in scar tissue rather than a cancer-like trophoblast. They also say further research is required on the uteroplacental interface (Nature Reviews Disease Primers 2025;11:40; DOI 10.1038/s41572-025-00624-3; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40473652/, abstract). High-probability cases “can be generally identified by prenatal ultrasonography,” and management is multidisciplinary surgery, not regeneration. Restoring an unscarred wall would be valuable. It is a better repair of an existing operation, concentrated in repeat cesarean with abnormal placental location, not a new principle of reproduction. Prenatal diagnosis and planned surgery already address much of the lethal surprise. Uncertainty remains: a later method that truly returned cesarean uteri to nulliparous strength at population scale could be reconsidered. The evidence checked here does not put it over the bar.

original_dispositions.original_title: Root-cause cure of polycystic ovary syndrome
original_dispositions.reason: Not added. The 2023 international guideline states that “PCOS aetiology is complex” and the presentation is heterogeneous, with reproductive, metabolic, and psychological features. Letrozole is recommended as first-line ovulation induction, with other fertility treatments after that (Teede and colleagues, Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism 2023;108:2447; DOI 10.1210/clinem/dgad463; https://academic.oup.com/jcem/article/108/10/2447/7242360, summary and infertility section). Fertility can often be restored without curing a single upstream lesion. A permanent metabolic cure that also prevents diabetes and cardiovascular disease would need further breakthroughs and was not treated as one obstetric discovery.

Not added. The central advance is male reproductive physiology, not obstetrics and gynecology. Highly effective contraception for people who can become pregnant already exists. A male method would share responsibility and could reduce unintended pregnancy. That is an equity and andrology goal, not a missing obstetric principle.

original_dispositions.original_title: Early noninvasive detection and prevention of ovarian cancer
original_dispositions.reason: Covered by OBG-09 for the unachieved revolutionary piece: fertility-preserving interception that reduces deaths. The screening-only half of the historical item is not added. UKCTOCS already showed earlier detection without fewer deaths.
Covered by OBG-08. Donor transplantation with live birth is an achieved component and is not the breakthrough.

reconciliation_change_log.reason: OBG-01, OBG-04, and OBG-10 are three different routes to preterm birth. OBG-02 and OBG-05 both touch age-related fertility and remain different capabilities. OBG-03 and OBG-08 are different answers to gestation without a working uterus. OBG-09 is not a demand for a high-sensitivity screening test.

reconciliation_change_log.reason: The ACOG “Women’s Health 2030” URL returns a 404 (https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2025/01/womens-health-2030). The SMFM “Research Priorities 2025–2030” URL returns a 404 (https://www.smfm.org/research-priorities-2025). The Nature Reviews DOI 10.1038/s41572-025-00812-3 returns “Page Not Found” (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41572-025-00812-3). A real 2025 primer in that journal is the placenta accreta review, DOI 10.1038/s41572-025-00624-3, which is a different paper. The cited Lancet commission URL could not be opened, and no finished “Lancet Commission on Women’s and Reproductive Health 2025” listing these ten discoveries was found. What does exist is the Countdown to 2030 progress report (Lancet 2025;405:1505–1554; https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(25)00151-5/fulltext) and an announcement of a new Lancet Commission on Maternal and Newborn Health (DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(25)02599-1; https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(25)02599-1/fulltext). AJOG in November 2026 is volume 235, issue 5 (https://www.ajog.org/current). A “Vision 2030 for OB/GYN Research” special issue was not found.
